questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a use case in UML modeling?

options.A: To define the internal algorithms of a system component.
options.B: To describe interactions between users (or other systems) and the system.
options.C: To specify the hardware requirements for deployment.
options.D: To list all classes that will be implemented.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Use cases are used to describe interactions between users and a system, as stated in the context describing use cases as a way of describing interactions [Page 25].

---

questions.question: According to the provided guidelines, which of the following should **not** be used when writing user requirements?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The text advises that user requirements should avoid software jargon, structured notations, or formal notations [Page 20].

---

questions.question: In the Mentcare system use‑case diagram (Figure 4.15), which actor is most likely responsible for the “Edit record” use case?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Medium] The picture text lists “Edit record” alongside the “Doctor” actor, indicating that the Doctor performs that use case [Page 25].

---

questions.question: Which statement best captures the relationship between a use case and its textual description?

options.A: The textual description is optional and rarely linked to other models.
options.B: The textual description provides a detailed, natural‑language narrative that can be linked to other UML models for deeper detail.
options.C: The textual description must contain formal UML syntax.
options.D: The textual description only lists system performance metrics.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The material states that each use case should be documented with a textual description and can be linked to other UML models to develop the scenario in more detail [Page 25].

---

questions.question: The concept of use cases was first introduced in which development method?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Use cases were first introduced in the Objectory method [Page 25].

---

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an actor in the Mentcare system use‑case diagram?
questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The diagram lists “Nurse” as one of the actors interacting with the system [Page 25].

questions.question: Linking a documented use case to other UML models primarily helps to:

options.A: Reduce the number of required test cases.
options.B: Provide a more detailed view of the scenario’s behavior and structure.
options.C: Eliminate the need for a sequence diagram.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The context explains that linking use cases to other UML models develops the scenario in more detail [Page 25].

---

questions.question: Which of the following is **not** a characteristic of good user requirements according to the text?

options.B: Presented with simple tables and intuitive diagrams.
options.C: Contains software‑specific jargon and formal notation.
options.D: Focuses on the user’s perspective rather than technical implementation.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] The passage explicitly advises against using software jargon, structured notations, or formal notations when writing user requirements [Page 20].

---

questions.question: If a sequence diagram shows several objects interacting during a use‑case implementation, what can be inferred about the system?

options.A: The system has no dynamic behavior.
options.B: The use case involves multiple components that collaborate at runtime.
options.C: The system’s database schema is fully defined.
options.D: The use case is purely static and does not involve any objects.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] The context indicates that a sequence diagram reveals the objects or components involved in the interaction, implying collaborative runtime behavior [Page 49].
